articles.title: Shane Lowry: Irish golfer links up with Rory McIlroy in first ever TGL trade
articles.summary: Shane Lowry is the first player to be traded in the TMRW Golf League (TGL) as he joins Rory McIlroy at Boston Common Golf for 2027.
articles.body:
Shane Lowry is the first player to be traded in the TMRW Golf League (TGL) and will join Rory McIlroy at Boston Common Golf for 2027.

Ireland's Lowry makes the move before the third season of TGL, which takes place at the SoFi Centre in Florida and comprises traditional golf with technology.

The 39-year-old spent the first two seasons at The Bay GC, and he will now link up with five-time major winner McIlroy as team rosters expand to five players for the new campaign.

USA Ryder Cup captain Keegan Bradley and Masters champions Adam Scott and Hideki Matsuyama joined McIlroy at Boston Common Golf last season.

In a trade for Lowry, The Bay will acquire Boston Common Golf's fourth draft selection to fill its open roster spot, as well as one future selection over the next three seasons and commercial considerations.

McIlroy, who co-founded TGL alongside Tiger Woods and Mike McCarley, said 2019 Open champion Lowry is a "great friend" and he loves playing alongside him.

"We've had some special wins together, including at the Zurich Classic, and I know the quality of his game and how much he cares about winning for his team-mates," he added.

"I'm delighted to welcome him to Boston Common Golf and excited about what we can achieve together this season."

Lowry, who won the Irish Open at Doonbeg in September, added he was "delighted" to make the move to link up with McIlroy for the new campaign.

"Having Rory alongside me and being part of this group makes it particularly exciting, and I'm looking forward to helping the team bring a championship to Boston," he said.

Elsewhere in the league, new team Motor City Golf Club announced five-time major winner Brooks Koepka as its first player.

articles.title: Tiger Woods, Rory McIlroy, Justin Thomas, Brooks Koepka Headline 2027 TGL Rosters
articles.summary: TGL announced each of the seven teams for its 2027 seasons, with each roster growing from four to five golfers.
articles.body:
TGL announced each of the seven teams for its 2027 seasons, with each roster growing from four to five golfers.

Tiger Woods (Jupiter Links GC), Rory McIlroy (Boston Common Golf) and Cameron Young (New York GC) are among the returnees. Brooks Koepka, Si Woo Kim and Jackson Koivun will play starring roles on the expansion Motor City GC.

Front Office Sports' David Rumsey noted Xander Schauffele, Kevin Kisner, Adam Scott, and Lucas Glover won't take part after competing in 2026.

Defending champion Los Angeles GC is running it back with Collin Morikawa, Justin Rose, Tommy Fleetwood and Sahith Theegala. The quartet combined to beat Jupiter Links GC 2-0 in the TGL Finals Series.

Former Virginia standout Ben James rounds out the team. A first-team All-American, he finished atop the PGA Tour University standings for the 2025-26 season to earn a PGA Tour card.

Once again, the runners-up are likely to garner the most fascination in TGL.

Woods missed nearly the entire 2026 season and only represented Jupiter Links in the Finals Series. Injuries and personal issues have significantly limited how much the 15-time champion has competed in recent years.

Even at this stage of his career, Woods remains one of the biggest names in golf. Fans will be eager to see how much he appears in TGL and what it could mean for any larger comeback.

In the case of James and Koivun, TGL will be a preview of what to expect ahead of their first full seasons on the tour.

Koivun turned pro ahead of the John Deere Classic in July. He was victorious in just his third start at the 3M Open and went on to represent the United States as it won the Presidents Cup.

articles.title: See the 16 teams of LPGA, PGA Tour stars competing at 2026 Grant Thornton Invitational
articles.summary: The teams have been made official for one of the most beloved events in golf's "silly season."
articles.body:
One of the most beloved events of golf's "silly season" has announced new details. The 2026 Grant Thornton Invitational returns to Tiburon Golf Club in Naples, Florida, Dec. 11-13, and the teams were made official Tuesday.

Each pair features one active LPGA player and one active PGA Tour player who will compete together in a fun, three-day competition featuring three separate formats. Day 1 is a scramble, Day 2 is alternate shot, and Day 3 is "modified four-ball," where each player tees off, then switches balls and plays their partner's ball until they finish the hole.

Lauren Coughlin and Andrew Novak are back to defend their title. A year ago, the American duo shot 28 under to win the tournament by three shots. Some other familiar pairings have joined forces again, like Lydia Ko and Jason Day, who won the inaugural Grant Thornton Invitational in 2023, as well as Patty Tavatanakit and Jake Knapp, the 2024 champions.

But there are also quite a few new duos set to tee it up at Tiburon together. World No. 1 Nelly Korda will play alongside Michael Brennan, who was paired with Charley Hull last year. Hull is unable to play this time around because she'll be attending fellow LPGA star Georgia Hall's wedding, she told Golfweek in a recent Q&A.

Another new pairing that is sure to raise some eyebrows is the duo of American young guns Kiara Romero and Jackson Koivun, both of whom are former world No. 1 amateurs who recently turned pro.

articles.title: Kerby Joseph injury: Lions expect All-Pro safety to return this season
articles.summary: Dan Campbell expects Lions safety Kerby Joseph to return this season as he recovers from a lingering knee injury.
articles.body:
ALLEN PARK — Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said Tuesday, Oct. 20, that he expects All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph to play this season.

Campbell wasn't willing to set a timetable for Joseph's return but sounded genuinely optimistic about his recovery, even as Joseph passes a full year since he last stepped onto the field.

"I do," Campbell said plainly when asked if he expects Joseph to play this season.

Joseph has battled a lingering knee injury since last year's training camp, which forced him out of the final 11 games of last season. Campbell hasn't been as optimistic about his chances of returning when asked over the last few months about the future of Joseph, one of the best free safeties in the game. Joseph recorded 20 interceptions in 55 games from 2022-25.

"He's doing well. I'll leave it at that," Campbell said. "He really is, he's doing a good job. I'm not gonna give you a timetable, but I've been pleased where he's at. He's in a good headspace right now, which is great. Because that's hard. You're coming off this, you're wanting to go, you're working at it, and at some point it's time for football. We all know that and recognize it, but we'll take it one day at a time."

The Lions ' defense has sorely missed their elite safety tandem. Brian Branch has also been on the shelf since Dec. 2025 because of a torn Achilles that ended his season. The Lions currently own the league's last-ranked passing defense (297.4 yards per game) entering Week 7, in part because two of their biggest gamebreakers haven't been on the field.

The team expects Branch to play against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday, Oct. 25, at Ford Field.

articles.title: 'Trash Island' or DC landmark? Golfers weigh in on Trump's plans to change course
articles.summary: Trump said he has plans to turn a 106-year-old public golf course in Washington DC into a tournament-capable golf course for pros, but local golfers are not happy.
articles.body:
For Jourdain Yardan, golfing at the East Potomac Golf Links on Washington DC's waterfront is a twice-weekly ritual.

"Anyone from any walk of life, whether they're starting to play golf or whether they're a ... seasoned golfer, they can come out here and play golf at a pretty reasonable rate," the 35-year-old told the BBC while putting on the course on Monday.

But President Donald Trump does not seem convinced of its charms, calling the 106-year-old course "Trash Island" Monday evening on Truth Social.

Now, he intends to shut it down for renovations to create a space that "will be open to the Public while, at the same time, designed to the Highest Level of Golf and able to hold World Class Tournaments".

The renovation is part of the president's sprawling and controversial efforts to shape the US capital, which include a new White House ballroom, a 250-foot-tall arch and other changes to longstanding landmarks. The golf course is a smaller project, but deeply personal to many who live in the city.

Yardan described a potential shuttering, even if temporary, as a "huge dent" in DC culture that could change the heart of the space.

Trump, an avid golfer and owner of more than a dozen courses, says his vision for the course will make it "one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World".

But courts will need to mediate the dispute between the White House and the community before Trump can realize his plans.

The historic course, which sits 2 miles (3km) south of the White House, is one of three public courses run by the National Park Service in the nation's capital. A lawsuit from the DC Preservation League and two golfers from the course asks the court to stop Trump's planned renovation.

"Our litigation is intended to protect this community jewel for the people and communities it serves," Democracy Forward, the group representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement on social media.

The legal fight intensified this month after the government began large-scale tree removal on the course without giving the court or plaintiffs notice.

A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to stop its redevelopment plans until at least 26 October.

Despite the work stoppage, Trump took to social media on Sunday to announce that the course will be closed for 15-months beginning in November to accommodate the renovations. He also shared a rendering of the course redesign.

"The current Course is old, broken, dilapidated, and of no further use or effect. It is in very poor condition, with falling, dangerous, and disease-infested trees and, importantly, a collapsing and hazardous seawall," Trump wrote in his post on Sunday.

While golfer Thomas Snow, who is not part of the suit, conceded the course could use a "facelift", he thinks the president's description of the course is a "gross overstatement".

Currently, East Potomac does not offer the manicured experience one might find at the luxury, private golf courses the president is known for building. The public course is open to all and does not require a membership to access.

The facilities at the DC course are more modest, offering food court-style dining rather than amenities such as white tablecloth restaurants and upscale locker rooms.

Golfers like Snow and Yardan who regularly play the courses at East Potomac, told the BBC it offers a rare combination of affordability and proximity to the city.

"You start to clear everything out and it just starts to become an empty plot of land that you just hit golf balls on; I think it gets rid of the culture of the golf course," Yardan said.

As a 70-year-old golfer, Snow pays $29 (£21.65) for 18 holes when he visits East Potomac.

"There's no place in the whole DMV (the metropolitan region including DC and its Maryland and Virginia suburbs) that you can play a nice 18 holes for that price point," he said.

Snow worries that if Trump's proposal moves forward, people will be priced out.

Yardan, the twice-weekly golfer, echoed those concerns.

"Anytime you hear about big league, big golfers, that also includes big prices," he said. "The biggest thing that I like about this golf course .. is that it's affordable," he said.

images.caption: Jourdain Yardan worries regular people will not be able to golf at the course if it is renovated as Trump suggested

articles.title: Green Bay Packers: Matt LaFleur on roughing calls and Jordan Love
articles.summary: Green Bay Packers coach Matt LaFleur said Monday that Jordan Love is not getting roughing-the-passer calls and should push officials harder for them. The Pac...
articles.body:
Green Bay Packers coach Matt LaFleur said Monday that Jordan Love is not getting roughing-the-passer calls and should push officials harder for them.

The Packers were flagged for roughing the passer three times in the fourth quarter of Sunday's 23-13 win over the Dallas Cowboys . Dallas was not flagged for it once. Love was sacked three times, and the official game book credits Dallas with eight quarterback hits.

LaFleur said he wants the rule enforced the same way for both teams.

"At the end of the day, you just want it to be called both ways," LaFleur said. "So if they're going to call it one way, it should be called for the other team as well. And I feel like there's been a lot of times when Jordan's taken some close to potential roughing calls. He's not getting the calls."

"I don't know. I think he needs to be more of an a-hole to the officials or lobby for some of those calls," LaFleur continued. "You see some guys do it, and it works."

The Green Bay Packers were flagged for roughing three times in the fourth quarter

The first call cost Green Bay an interception. Carrington Valentine picked off Dak Prescott at the Green Bay 34 with 7:44 left and returned it 21 yards, but Lukas Van Ness was flagged for roughing on the play.

LaFleur did not think the Van Ness hit was a foul.

"What's the definition? You get like a step before you have to hit the quarterback," LaFleur said. "And I didn't think it was a forceful hit to the quarterback."

Later on the same drive, a roughing call on defensive lineman Karl Brooks wiped out an incompletion and moved Dallas from the Green Bay 27 to the 13. The Cowboys turned it over on downs at the 14 on that drive.

The third came with 1:03 left, when Evan Williams was flagged on a 7-yard completion, moving the ball to the 6. Prescott threw a 6-yard touchdown pass to Ryan Flournoy two plays later.

The Brooks hit "did look like body weight," LaFleur said, and the staff did not agree on another of the calls.

"I know there was some discussion amongst that play with the staff in regards to whether or not it was roughing," LaFleur said. "So I think some guys saw it one way, some guys saw it another way."

The Packers send plays to the league for review after every game.

"It helps us educate our players, and at the end of the day, that's our job," LaFleur said. "We've got to educate them on what they can and cannot do and make sure that we try to coach them up, and they've got to control themselves in the moment."

After the game Sunday, LaFleur called the total "far too many" and said the penalties were costly .

Matt LaFleur says Jordan Love "balled out" against Dallas

Love completed 23 of 41 passes for 276 yards, a touchdown and an interception and ran for a 1-yard score before halftime. LaFleur, who called Love "a G" after the game , went further Monday.

"I thought he balled out, and specifically yesterday. I thought he balled out," LaFleur said. "He played about as good as you could have played and taking hits in the process."

"For him to be able to stand in there, especially after some of the abuse he took early on in the season, I think it's a testament to him and his ability and just how tough-minded of a guy he is," LaFleur continued. "But he's doing a great job getting the ball out of his hands. He's trusting his guys to go make plays for him."

Standing in against pressure was a requirement when the Packers scouted quarterbacks, LaFleur said.

"Usually the old chuck-and-duck isn't too good for anybody," LaFleur said.

Love said Sunday the hits come with the job.

"As part of playing the quarterback job, you know, you got to be able to stand in that pocket and take some hits and still deliver balls," Love said.

The Packers (4-2) play at the Detroit Lions on Sunday, Oct. 25, at 3:25 p.m. CT on FOX.
